title: Building PCBs in America with a factory-scale robot
excerpt: The Grid builds U.S. circuit boards in four days for $630, beating Shenzhen quick-turn shops on speed despite a modest price premium.
body:
A 4-layer motor controller with 118 parts per board (38 unique) arrived from The Grid in four days for $630, while the same five-board order from a typical quick-turn shop in Shenzhen took nine days and cost $465 after shipping and U.S. tariffs. The price gap is about $165, but the time saved translates into five extra days of engineering work, a trade-off most hardware teams find worthwhile.

The Grid swaps the classic fixed assembly line for a single, factory-scale robot that carries each board along its own path. Because there is no line to reconfigure, changeovers disappear and domestic shipping replaces overseas freight. The result is a supply chain that can keep pace with rapid design iterations without the customs headaches that usually accompany offshore production.

## One robot replaces an entire line

Traditional PCB factories consist of a sequence of stations that must be manually retuned whenever a new design arrives. Retooling can consume hours, which is why many companies either outsource to low-cost labor or accept long lead times. The Grid eliminates that line entirely. A levitating mover transports each board and its components between machines that print solder paste, place parts, reflow, solder and inspect.

Since the robot is the only moving element, every board follows a unique route. A batch of 100 different designs runs as smoothly as 100 identical boards, and prototypes share the same equipment as low-volume production runs. No extra setup is required when a design changes.

## AI-driven scheduling keeps the flow smooth

Without intelligent scheduling, a single robot could quickly become a bottleneck. The Grid combines learned models, AI agents and classic optimization algorithms to decide which board goes where and when. Real-time routing balances machine capacity, part availability and delivery deadlines.

AI agents excel at handling the high-mix nature of the workload, while classic optimizers fine-tune timing to avoid peaks and valleys. The combined approach keeps every machine busy and prevents the stalls that plague manual lines.

## Concrete cost and lead-time comparison

The source provides a clear side-by-side example. Five assembled copies of the motor controller board, parts included, cost $630 and arrived in four days when built on The Grid. The same order from a typical Shenzhen quick-turn shop cost about $465 after shipping and U.S.

tariffs and took nine days to reach the same address. The Grid is roughly $165 more expensive, but it shaves off five days of engineering time and removes customs complications. For most hardware teams, five days of iteration time outweighs the modest price premium.

## High-mix, low-volume runs finally get automation

Most products never reach the million-unit volumes that justify dedicated production lines. Companies often need ten of one part, a hundred of another, and a new revision the next week. That “high-mix, low-volume” pattern has resisted automation because each new design traditionally required manual changeovers.

The Grid’s robot sidesteps that cost by treating every board as a unique job on a shared platform. Start-ups, large EV makers, AI labs and other tech firms already use the system for test stations, tooling, R&D and small production batches. Running prototypes and production on the same machines keeps design cycles short and supply chains domestic.

## The takeaway

Automation can serve high-mix, low-volume PCB orders when the factory revolves around a single, flexible robot instead of a fixed line. The Grid demonstrates that a domestic, robot-driven flow delivers boards in roughly half the time of a typical Shenzhen quick-turn shop, with only a modest cost increase. Teams that value engineering speed and supply-chain reliability should consider a robot-centric production model to get more time back for design work.  

*Source: [CircuitHub, Unveiling The Grid](https://www.circuithub.com/post/unveiling-the-grid)*
